source: Sztyber-Betley, Chanthery, Trave-Massuyes, Merkelbach, Kukla, Glotin, Diedrich, Niggemann (2025) Are Diagnostic Concepts Within the Reach of LLMs? (DX 2025)
finding: First paper to test LLMs on core MBD steps: build the incidence matrix, find MSO sets, find minimal conflicts, then minimal diagnoses (minimal hitting sets of conflicts). Ground truth came from the Fault Diagnosis Toolbox and a hitting-set program.
numbers: 23 arithmetic and logic circuits (adders, multipliers, AND/OR/NOR/NAND/XOR). Up to 15 relations, 6 MSOs, 6 conflicts, 165 diagnoses per example. Models gpt-4o-mini (with code interpreter), o1, o3-mini. 10 repeats for 4o-mini and o3-mini, o1 only once (about 30 USD per iteration). Each step scored with the correct input from the earlier step.
quote: At this point, LLMs do not provide an alternative to diagnosis algorithms.
limits: Small, hand-made circuits. All inputs and outputs assumed measured. Component faults only, no sensor faults. OpenAI models only.
agent_relevance: Direct test of whether a model can do Reiter-style diagnosis by itself. The answer is partly, so the scaffold should let code do the hitting-set step.

source: Sztyber-Betley et al. (2025) DX 2025, incidence-matrix step
finding: Building the equation-variable incidence matrix is easy for the reasoning models and hard for the weak model. o1 and o3-mini were perfect. 4o-mini kept adding known variables and faults as if they were unknowns.
numbers: o1 and o3-mini: F1 1.00 +/- 0.00, accuracy 1.00. 4o-mini: F1 0.47 +/- 0.15, strict accuracy 0.00 +/- 0.00.
limits: 4o-mini error is a format or concept slip (known vs unknown variables), not a logic failure. Footnote: plain gpt-4o and gpt-4o-mini without the interpreter had accuracy close to zero on unseen examples.
agent_relevance: Model-building from a system description is reliable only with a strong reasoning model or a code tool. A cheap model needs a code check on this step (G2, G3).

source: Sztyber-Betley et al. (2025) DX 2025, conflicts and diagnoses
finding: o3-mini was surprisingly good at conflicts and diagnoses, but diagnosis quality fell clearly as the number of diagnoses and relations grew. o1 was best on conflicts and on MSO sets, o3-mini best on diagnoses.
numbers: o3-mini conflicts F1 0.917 +/- 0.249. o3-mini diagnoses F1 0.784 +/- 0.322. The large standard deviations show wide spread across examples and runs. Largest examples had 153 to 165 diagnoses.
limits: Examples were written by hand and the correct answers were published after the models were released, so contamination is unlikely. Reasoning effort was high for the dedicated approach and medium for the broad approach.
agent_relevance: Enumerating diagnoses is the weakest step and grows combinatorially. Our agent should compute hitting sets in code and use the model only for conflict proposals.

source: Sztyber-Betley et al. (2025) DX 2025, prompt knowledge test
finding: Putting much more domain knowledge in the prompt did not help. The dedicated approach (circuit-specific prompts) and the broad approach (generic MSO prompt) scored about the same. Giving the correct incidence matrix as input to the MSO step also made no significant difference.
numbers: Compared in the MSO F1/precision/recall bars for three models and two prompt styles. 4o-mini was worst, o1 best across all metrics.
limits: Only two prompt designs per model. The paper gives bar charts, not a significance test.
agent_relevance: Longer, richer prompts do not buy diagnosis skill. Model strength and tool use matter more. Supports keeping the scaffold thin.

source: Sztyber-Betley et al. (2025) DX 2025, discussion
finding: Authors list the practical limits: accuracy too low to replace diagnosis tools, run time not boundable over an API, cost, and large run-to-run variation. Performance of o1 and o3-mini dropped as the number of relations rose, while 4o-mini with code interpreter stayed flat but low.
numbers: o1 evaluated once only; 4o-mini and o3-mini 10 times. Conflict trend lines rise with complexity only because zero-conflict cases (no inconsistency) are scored badly.
limits: The rising trend for conflicts is an artefact of the zero-conflict cases, so do not read it as skill growing with complexity.
agent_relevance: The model tends to invent conflicts when the observation fits the model. Our agent needs a code check that a claimed conflict is really violated (G2, G3).

source: Sztyber-Betley et al. (2025) DX 2025, related work on LLM diagnosis
finding: The paper reviews other LLM fault-diagnosis work and says none of it links LLM results to MBD concepts. Cited items: LLM plus physics-based tool for nuclear plant explanations; AutoFL; LLMAO; FD-LLM; FaultExplainer; FLEX; FaultLines; AAD-LLM. FaultExplainer is reported to depend on PCA-selected features and to hallucinate in places.
numbers: No numbers given in this survey paragraph. Seen as the authors' description, not checked in the originals.
limits: Secondhand description of the cited papers. Not opened one by one, except AutoFL (see b23).
agent_relevance: Confirms the gap: almost no published LLM test of consistency-based diagnosis with conflicts and hitting sets. Our scaffold would be among the first.

source: Gainer-Dewar and Vera-Licona (2016) The minimal hitting set generation problem: algorithms and computation
finding: Reiter 1987 introduced the hitting-set tree. Greiner et al. 1989 showed it is incomplete: its sets are minimal but some minimal hitting sets can be missed. The repair, HS-DAG, gives up the tree for a directed acyclic graph. Wotawa 2001 reworked it back into a tree (HST) with fewer containment checks.
numbers: Reiter 1987, Greiner et al. 1989 (HS-DAG), Wotawa 2001 (HST). The authors know of no formal complexity analysis of HS-DAG or HST.
quote: this algorithm is incomplete; the hitting sets it generates are guaranteed to be minimal, but in certain circumstances some MHSes may be missed
limits: A secondary review. The original 1987 and 1989 papers were not opened.
agent_relevance: The founding algorithm in the reading list had a real bug that stood for two years. Do not trust a model-written hitting-set routine without checking it against a reference (G3).

source: Gainer-Dewar and Vera-Licona (2016) benchmark of hitting-set algorithms
finding: Re-running published hitting-set algorithms and comparing their outputs found errors in several published implementations. MMCS and RS (Murakami and Uno 2014) and HTC-BDD (Bailey and Stuckey line, 2014) were far faster than the older diagnosis algorithms across many input families.
numbers: HTC-BDD beat its closest rivals by a factor of 4 to 10 on many inputs but often used up the 32 GB of memory and has no cutoff mode. MMCS and RS need very little memory and support cutoff and full enumeration. Test machine: 8 cores, 16 threads, 32 GB.
limits: Benchmarks come from Sudoku, data mining and biology set families, not only diagnosis. Some slightly wrong implementations were still timed.
agent_relevance: For the hitting-set step the agent should call a vetted solver, not ask the model to enumerate. This is a clean case for program-decides, model-fills (section 1 of the schema).

source: Jannach, Schmitz, Shchekotykhin (2016) Parallel Model-Based Diagnosis on Multi-Core Computers, JAIR 55
finding: Parallelising Reiter's hitting-set search speeds up diagnosis on standard DX Competition 2011 synthetic benchmarks. Full parallelisation (FP) beat level-wise parallelisation (LWP).
numbers: Four threads, all-diagnoses search: speedups 2.28 to 3.75. Sequential vs a parallel scheme significant (p<=0.05) in 95 of 100 scenarios. FP vs LWP significant in 59 of 100. FP gains more on harder problems because node-generation time dominates thread-sync cost.
limits: Gains depend on conflict-detection cost. Easy problems gain little.
agent_relevance: Shows how expensive consistency checks drive the search; cheap checks (code) are the bottleneck to protect, not the model's reasoning.

source: Jannach, Schmitz, Shchekotykhin (2016) JAIR 55, thread scaling
finding: More threads help up to the number of hardware cores, then stop. Efficiency drops as threads rise because of synchronisation.
numbers: 12-core server, FP with 4, 8, 10, 12 threads: speedups up to 5.20 (81 percent shorter run). 8 beat 4 on all five systems; 10 beat 8 on all but one; 12 was fastest on 3 of 5. More threads than cores gave nothing.
limits: Five DXC systems only.
agent_relevance: A boundary condition: parallel hypothesis testing has a ceiling set by the worker pool. Relevant if our agent tests many candidate faults at once.

source: Jannach, Schmitz, Shchekotykhin (2016) JAIR 55, single-diagnosis search and MXP
finding: Finding just one diagnosis (parallel depth-first search) sped up in most cases but not trivial ones. A better conflict finder (MXP, returns several conflicts per call) beat the basic one (QXP).
numbers: Single diagnosis: at least one parallel method significantly faster in 88 of 100 scenarios; the other 12 were too easy. MXP vs QXP sequential: 17 to 44 percent shorter. FP with MXP: speedup 1.33 to 2.10 (up to 52 percent shorter), and 38 to 76 percent faster than sequential QXP overall.
limits: Depth-first single-diagnosis search is faster but gives no guarantee of the best diagnosis.
agent_relevance: Getting more than one conflict per check is the biggest lever. Our agent should ask each failing check to return a full minimal conflict, not a single fault guess.

source: Jannach, Schmitz, Shchekotykhin (2016) JAIR 55, introduction
finding: Summarises the lineage: Reiter 1987 gave the logical theory of diagnosis from first principles and a breadth-first tree algorithm. MBD later spread to knowledge bases, ontologies, process specs, feature models, and software including VHDL, Java and spreadsheets. In many of these, one consistency check is costly, which is why hypotheses testing is the bottleneck.
numbers: No experimental numbers in the intro.
limits: Citing review, not the 1992 Readings book itself. Hamscher, Console, de Kleer 1992 was not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports reusing the same loop (propose, test consistency, hit conflicts) for code and spreadsheet debugging, which links to subfield 10.

source: Ignatiev, Morgado, Marques-Silva (2017) Model Based Diagnosis of Multiple Observations with Implicit Hitting Sets
finding: Analysing each failing observation on its own fails to scale. Treating many observations together with implicit hitting set dualization (IHSD) works fast and recovers the same diagnoses.
numbers: 1140 generated buggy-encoder CNF instances (observations r 10 to 300, parameter k 2 to 300). IHSD solved all, largest in about 0.1 s. Separate analysis with LBX or RS fully enumerated only 177 and 185 instances (those with k<8).
limits: Instances are synthetic and built to show the effect. The authors say complete enumeration of all subset-minimal diagnoses is in general infeasible, which is why minimum-size diagnoses are studied.
agent_relevance: When the agent sees many failing checks, it should pool the conflicts and hit them together, not diagnose each failure alone.

source: Ignatiev et al. (2017) arXiv 1707.01972, aggregated-formula test
finding: Merging all observations into one big formula blows up formula size by orders of magnitude, so it is also not a fix.
numbers: At r=500, k=2000: IHSD formula 6,510 variables and 8,506 clauses, 0.49 s. Aggregated: 3,269,512 variables and 4,261,506 clauses, LBX 6.15 s and RS 6.33 s (formula build time not counted). At r=10,k=10 all methods take about 0.01 s.
limits: The authors say the example is made as simple as possible to show the effect.
agent_relevance: A size warning for any scaffold that stacks every observation into one context: cost grows fast. Prefer incremental conflict sets.

source: Feldman, Provan, van Gemund (2010) Approximate Model-Based Diagnosis Using Greedy Stochastic Search (SAFARI), JAIR 38
finding: A greedy random search (SAFARI) gives up completeness and optimality to find multiple-fault diagnoses on circuits where exact methods time out. It solved every test on the 74XXX and ISCAS85 suites while complete methods CDA and HA solved few large ones.
limits: Quality of the answer is only near-optimal. Test sets contain mostly single- and double-fault observations for the optimality check.
agent_relevance: Strong precedent for an anytime, stochastic search that returns a decent diagnosis fast. Fits an agent with a token budget.

source: Feldman, Provan, van Gemund (2010) JAIR 38, optimality analysis
finding: For weak-fault models (ignorance of abnormal behaviour) SAFARI returns near-minimal cardinality diagnoses. For strong-fault models quality drops on larger circuits when retries are few. The authors prove polynomial time for minimal-cardinality search in weak-fault models using only boundary constraint propagation, and model the search as a Markov chain to bound minimality.
numbers: Worst single-fault case c1355, hardest double-fault case c499. With strong-fault models, quality is close to optimal for small circuits and worsens from c3540 upward with the modest retries and flips used. More retries M and flips N improve it.
limits: They also construct models that make the optimality bound arbitrarily bad, so the method has no worst-case guarantee. Abstract of the 2008 AAAI paper calls the exact problem Sigma2-P hard.
agent_relevance: Fault models matter: a weak-fault (no fault-mode assumptions) setup is much easier to search. Keep the agent's fault models weak unless data says otherwise.

source: Feldman, Provan, van Gemund (2010) JAIR 38, model counting comparison
finding: Off-the-shelf model counting is not a substitute. RelSat solved only the two smallest circuits within the 1 hour limit. SampleCount gave lower bounds only up to c1355.
numbers: 1 hour limit per run; SampleCount default settings (alpha 3.5, t 2, z 20, cutoff 10,000 flips).
limits: Default solver settings only. Specialised encodings might do better.
agent_relevance: Counting-style shortcuts do not give diagnoses cheaply. Another reason to keep a purpose-built conflict loop.

source: Feldman, Provan, van Gemund (2008) Computing Minimal Diagnoses by Greedy Stochastic Search, AAAI-08
finding: Earlier conference version of SAFARI. Same claim: exact multiple-fault diagnosis is Sigma2-P hard, a greedy stochastic algorithm gives order-of-magnitude speedups over CDA and HA, with a probabilistic minimality bound.
numbers: Abstract and introduction read; the full tables were taken from the 2010 journal version instead (b15).
limits: Only the first page was read closely. The journal version supersedes it.
agent_relevance: Shows the idea was stable across versions, which is weak evidence of a replicated result inside one group, not by an outside group.

source: Wu, Li, Zhang, Papadakis, Harman, Liu (2023) Large Language Models in Fault Localisation
finding: ChatGPT-4 given a function plus the failing-test error log beats the best spectrum and mutation methods at function level, but loses badly when the context grows to a whole class.
numbers: Defects4J, six Java projects. Function level: mean Top-1 of 23.13, 46.9 percent higher than SmartFL. Class level: ChatGPT-4 is 49.9 percent worse than SmartFL. Dropping the error log cuts accuracy 25.6 percent, the largest ablation loss. Variance of Top-1 across repeats 12.00 percent for ChatGPT-4 with logs. New StuDefects set (programs from 2022 on): 52.9 percent better than state of the art.
limits: Defects4J may be in training data, the authors added StuDefects to check. The two ChatGPT models can change over time. Class-level collapse is the key boundary.
agent_relevance: Real failure output is the strongest single signal (supports G2). Context length hurts localisation, so feed the agent small pieces.

source: Wu et al. (2023) arXiv 2308.15276, repeats and ablation
finding: Five repeated runs showed ChatGPT-4 with logs was the top method in every repeat; removing any prompt component lowered ChatGPT-4's Top-1. Dynamic execution information made answers more consistent.
numbers: Five repeated experiments on Defects4J. Variance of Top-1 down to 12.00 percent for ChatGPT-4 (Log), lowest among the ChatGPT variants.
limits: Only two OpenAI models. Single dataset family plus one new small set.
agent_relevance: Run-to-run noise is real, but real execution data reduces it. Matches our rule to revise from actual output.

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) A Quantitative and Qualitative Evaluation of LLM-Based Explainable Fault Localization (AutoFL)
finding: An LLM that navigates the repository through function calls from one failing test beats spectrum-based fault localisation at first rank, but falls behind at ranks 3 and 5 with GPT-3.5.
numbers: 798 real bugs (Java Defects4J and Python BugsInPy). Method-level acc@1 over Ochiai: +19.7 percent on Defects4J with GPT-3.5, +166.7 percent on BugsInPy with GPT-3.5, +233.3 percent on BugsInPy with GPT-4. GPT-3.5 acc@3 and acc@5 lag SBFL; GPT-4 stays ahead up to acc@5.
limits: Author inspection: GPT-3.5 has trouble digging deep into a repository. SmartFL compared on a 222-bug subset only.
agent_relevance: A weak model wins on top-1 but is not a reliable ranker. A diagnostic ranking should come from code, not from model order.

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) AutoFL, explanation quality and confidence
finding: Manual check of explanations found most are wrong even when the location is right. Agreement across repeated runs is a usable confidence signal.
numbers: 300 explanations from 60 bugs checked by hand: about 20 percent accurately describe how the bug happened; 56.7 percent of bugs had at least one accurate description. Confidence = share of runs agreeing; higher confidence tends to go with better results.
limits: Self-consistency confidence is the same signal our guardrail G4 says is a hint, not proof (samples from one model are not independent).
agent_relevance: Localising a fault and explaining it are different skills. Use agreement only to rank, then verify with a check.

source: Tyen, Mansoor, Carbune, Chen, Mak (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Finding where a chain-of-thought went wrong is the hard part. Models are weak at locating the faulty step even on clear, objective tasks.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake: 2,186 chain-of-thought traces across five tasks. Best model GPT-4 reaches 52.87 overall mistake-location accuracy with direct step-level prompting. Per-task scores for several models fell as low as 1.67 to 10.10 (GPT-3.5-Turbo).
limits: Traces are from PaLM 2 on algorithmic tasks, not circuits. Mistake-finding test sets were sampled to be 85 percent wrong traces and 15 percent right ones.
agent_relevance: This is a diagnosis problem in model reasoning itself. Locating the fault step needs code or a trained classifier, not self-judgment (G2).

source: Tyen et al. (2024) arXiv 2311.08516, correction given location
finding: If told which step is wrong, models fix traces well. Wrong locations hurt. A locator that is only 60 to 70 percent accurate was already enough for backtracking to help on most tasks.
numbers: Backtracking with true mistake location: wrong-answer traces gain between 18.04 and 43.92 points across tasks, right-answer traces lose 0 to 11.43 points. With a random location: gains only 5.16 to 21.57 points and losses up to 15.91 points.
limits: Gold mistake labels are rarely available. Experiments on five tasks. Number of right-answer traces is small.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence for the order: first locate the fault with an external check, then ask the model to repair that exact spot. This is the same split as MBD conflict then repair.

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without outside feedback, asking a model to review and fix its own answer lowers reasoning accuracy. Gains reported earlier came from using the ground-truth label to decide when to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 standard vs after 2 correction rounds: GSM8K 75.9 to 74.7; CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 to 43.0. With oracle labels GPT-3.5: 84.3, 89.7, 29.0; GPT-4: 97.5, 85.5, 59.0.
limits: Intrinsic self-correction only; adding feedback from tools or humans is not covered. HotpotQA sample was only 100 items.
agent_relevance: The classic failed-replication-style result for blind self-review. Supports G1 and G2: doubt only on a signal, revise only from real output.

source: Huang et al. (2024) arXiv 2310.01798, why self-correction fails
finding: When models do change an answer, they are more likely to turn a right answer into a wrong one than the reverse. The model cannot judge the correctness of its own reasoning.
numbers: GSM8K with GPT-3.5: the initial answer is kept 74.7 percent of the time. On CommonSenseQA the model changes answers more often, because wrong options look plausible.
limits: Number is for one model and one prompt family taken from earlier papers.
agent_relevance: Gives the mechanism behind G1. In MBD terms the model is both the test generator and the judge, so its judgments add noise.

source: Hamscher, Console, de Kleer (eds., 1992) Readings in Model-Based Diagnosis (Morgan Kaufmann)
finding: Standard reference collection. Not opened in this session. Its core papers (Reiter 1987, de Kleer and Williams 1987 GDE, de Kleer, Mackworth, Reiter 1992) were met here only through later papers: b07 (Reiter, Greiner correction, Wotawa), b12 (Jannach intro) and b01 (R-conflict and minimal diagnosis as minimal hitting set).
numbers: None read.
limits: Paywalled book. Do not cite numbers from it.
agent_relevance: Reading list is covered by proxy; the next step, if needed, is the Reiter 1987 and Greiner 1989 papers themselves.
